title: Some prescription medicines will get an extra charge from March 2027
summary: Japan plans a new extra charge for selected prescription medicines that can be substituted by OTC drugs, starting in March 2027. The current design uses an extra charge equal to 25% of the medicine price; medical-need exemptions are planned, while income category alone generally will not remove the charge.
why_it_matters: This can raise out-of-pocket costs for common medicines even when they are still prescribed through insurance. MHLW's September 4 position says affected low-income insured people are generally expected to pay the extra charge unless another exemption, such as medical necessity, applies.

claims.text: Japan has enacted a medical-insurance reform that creates a separate out-of-insurance charge for selected prescription medicines considered highly substitutable by OTC medicines.
claims.basis: MHLW reform and medical-insurance committee records

claims.text: MHLW is preparing the scheme for a March 2027 start, and on September 4 said the separate charge for people other than public-assistance recipients is set at one quarter of the medicine price to avoid an abrupt burden increase.
claims.basis: MHLW June 19 implementation timeline and September 4 minister briefing

claims.text: MHLW says exemptions are being prepared for medical-need situations including cancer or intractable-disease patients and people for whom long-term use of an affected medicine is medically necessary.
claims.basis: September 4 minister briefing and technical-review process

claims.text: On September 4, MHLW said it does not plan to exempt insured people uniformly based on income category; people using affected medicines are generally expected to pay the separate charge unless another exemption applies.
claims.basis: Minister response on treatment of low-income insured people

claims.text: Households that regularly use prescription medicines with OTC equivalents should prepare to check the final covered-drug and medical-need exemption rules before March 2027 rather than assuming current pharmacy payments will remain unchanged.
claims.basis: Enacted reform plus current implementation rules

content.key_message: A new prescription-drug charge is coming in March 2027; regular users of common OTC-like medicines should watch the final drug list and medical-need exemption rules.
what_changed: The underlying health-insurance reform is already enacted; implementation details are now being finalized.
MHLW's current design adds a separate charge equal to 25% of the medicine price for selected OTC-like prescription drugs.
MHLW said on September 4 that income category alone will not generally exempt insured people from the extra charge; separate medical-need exemptions are planned.
content.who_is_affected: People in Japan who receive prescription medicines that end up on the final OTC-like drug list. You are not automatically affected just because you use prescription medicine; the exact medicine and whether a medical-need exemption applies will matter.
content.when: MHLW is preparing implementation for March 2027. Final medicine-level operational details are still being finalized as of September 4, 2026.
content.financial_impact: Affected prescriptions would carry the usual insured patient share plus a separate charge based on 25% of the medicine price under the current design. The exact yen impact depends on the drug, quantity and final implementation rules.
content.risk_if_ignored: You may be surprised by a higher pharmacy bill in 2027 or incorrectly stop or alter a medically necessary medicine without first checking whether an exemption applies.
content.deadline: No consumer application deadline is announced. The meaningful checkpoint is before the planned March 2027 start, after MHLW publishes the final covered-drug and exemption rules.
content.potential_benefit: Avoid an unexpected pharmacy cost and know whether a medically necessary prescription qualifies for an exemption.
content.downside: There is little value in changing medicine now because the final covered list and detailed exemption operation are not yet fully settled.
content.skeptical_view: The reform does not mean all common prescriptions will suddenly become fully self-paid. The policy is a targeted extra charge while insurance coverage remains in place, and medical-need exemptions are part of the design. The final medicine list and operating details can still change before launch.
content.what_to_watch: Watch MHLW's medical-insurance reform and OTC-like-drug pages for the final covered-drug list, exemption criteria, patient examples and confirmed implementation details.
content.what_would_change_mind: ALAM would revise this guidance if MHLW changes the March 2027 timing, the 25% charge design, materially narrows or expands the covered medicines, or changes the exemption treatment for low-income or medically necessary use.
content.bottom_line: Do not change treatment now; if you use regular prescription medicines, check the final MHLW list and ask your doctor or pharmacist about exemption status before the March 2027 rollout.

30 sec: What happened: Japan is preparing an extra charge for selected prescription medicines that have close OTC alternatives.
Why it matters: the current design adds 25% of the medicine price on top of the normal insured patient share.
What to do: do not switch or stop medicine now; wait for the final MHLW list and exemption rules, then check regular prescriptions.
Bottom line: medical-need exemptions exist, but low income by itself generally will not remove the extra charge under MHLW's current position.
reading_levels.2_min: Japan's 2026 medical-insurance reform creates a new category for selected prescription medicines that are considered highly substitutable by over-the-counter medicines. Under the current implementation design, an affected prescription remains within the medical system but carries a separate charge equal to 25% of the medicine price in addition to the normal insured patient share. MHLW is preparing a March 2027 start. Exemptions are being designed for medically necessary cases such as some cancer, intractable-disease and long-term-use situations. On September 4, MHLW said low-income insured people will not be exempted uniformly simply because of income category; affected medicines are generally expected to carry the separate charge unless another exemption applies. The sensible action now is preparation, not self-directed switching.

outcomes: Understand what an OTC-like prescription medicine means.
Understand how the new extra charge differs from removing a medicine entirely from insurance.
Know why the final medical-need exemption rules matter before changing treatment.
learning.background: Japan distinguishes medical-use prescription medicines from OTC medicines sold directly to consumers. Some prescription products have the same or very similar active ingredients and uses as OTC products. The new reform creates a separate extra-payment mechanism for a selected subset judged especially substitutable by OTC medicine rather than simply declaring every such prescription uninsured.

terms.meaning: An over-the-counter medicine that can be bought without a prescription.
terms.why_it_matters: The reform targets selected prescription medicines for which an OTC alternative is considered highly substitutable.

terms.meaning: A payment outside the normal insured copay that is added when an affected medicine is prescribed.
terms.why_it_matters: It means the patient's pharmacy payment can rise even though the prescription still passes through insured medical care.

how_it_works.title: Normal prescription payment
how_it_works.explanation: A patient normally pays the insured copay percentage on the covered medicine and other eligible medical costs.

how_it_works.title: Affected OTC-like medicine
how_it_works.explanation: Under the current design, an affected medicine would also carry a separate charge based on one quarter of its medicine price.

how_it_works.title: Medical-need exception
how_it_works.explanation: If the final rules classify the patient's situation as medically necessary for exemption, that separate charge may not apply. Income category alone is not the general exemption rule MHLW described on September 4.

learning.example: Illustrative mechanism only: if an affected medicine's listed medicine cost were ¥1,000, the current design's separate charge would be based on ¥250. The patient's total bill is not simply ¥250 because the ordinary insured copay and other prescription costs are calculated separately. This example is for understanding the mechanism, not a quote for any specific drug.
takeaways: The reform is enacted; implementation is being finalized for March 2027.
It is an extra charge, not a blanket removal of every OTC-like medicine from insurance.
Medical-need exemptions can change whether the extra charge applies.
Low income alone generally will not remove the charge under MHLW's September 4 position.
Do not stop or switch prescribed medicine on your own to avoid a future fee.

action_plan.goal: Be ready to identify whether a regular prescription will be affected and whether a medical-need exemption applies once final rules are published.
action_plan.who_should_act: People in Japan who regularly receive prescription medicines, especially common medicines that may have OTC equivalents. People with no regular prescriptions can safely ignore this for now.
action_plan.deadline: Re-check before the planned March 2027 implementation. No consumer filing deadline has been announced.
prepare: A current medication list or medication notebook (お薬手帳)
Exact medicine names and strengths for medicines you take regularly
The reason each long-term medicine is prescribed, if known
Any official MHLW update showing the final covered-drug list or exemption rules

steps.action: Write down the exact names and strengths of medicines you receive repeatedly.
steps.how: Use your お薬手帳, pharmacy printout or prescription history.
needed: Medication list or お薬手帳
steps.done_when: You have an exact list rather than only symptoms or brand descriptions.

steps.step: Wait for the final official list
steps.action: Check MHLW's OTC-like-drug reform information once the final implementation list is published.
steps.how: Use the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare website or ask your pharmacist to verify the official list.
steps.done_when: Each regular medicine is marked affected, unaffected or still unclear from official information.

steps.action: If a regular medicine is affected, ask the prescribing doctor or pharmacist whether your use falls under the final medical-need exemption criteria.
steps.how: Bring the medication list and explain the treatment reason; rely on the final official criteria rather than social-media summaries.
steps.done_when: You know whether the extra charge is expected to apply to that prescription under the final rule.

steps.step: Compare safe options only with a professional
steps.action: If the charge applies, ask whether continuing the prescription, using an OTC alternative or another medically appropriate option makes sense.
steps.how: Discuss it with the prescribing doctor or pharmacist; do not self-switch chronic treatment solely for price.
steps.done_when: You have a medically appropriate plan for the first affected refill after rollout.

mistakes_to_avoid: Assuming every prescription with an OTC equivalent is automatically affected.
Treating the 25% figure as 25% of your entire clinic/pharmacy bill; it is tied to the affected medicine price under the current design.
Assuming resident-tax-exempt status automatically waives the charge; MHLW said on September 4 that it does not plan a uniform income-category exemption for insured people.
Stopping or reducing prescribed medicine without medical advice.
Buying a large OTC stockpile months early before the final list and rules are settled.

decision_rules.if: Your medicine is not on the final affected list
decision_rules.then: This specific extra charge does not apply to that medicine.

decision_rules.if: Your medicine is affected but your use meets a final medical-need exemption
decision_rules.then: Follow the exemption handling instructed by your doctor or pharmacist and official guidance.

decision_rules.if: Your medicine is affected and no exemption applies
decision_rules.then: Ask the pharmacist for the expected additional cost and discuss medically appropriate alternatives before changing treatment.

decision_rules.if: Final MHLW medicine-level rules are not yet published
decision_rules.then: Prepare your medication list and wait; do not alter treatment based on draft discussions.

action_plan.follow_up: Re-check MHLW guidance when the final covered-drug list and exemption criteria are released, and again shortly before the first refill after the rollout.
